Semantic-Condition Tuning: Fusing Graph Context with Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph Completion

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: International World Wide Web Conference 2026; April 13-17, 2026; Dubai, UAEISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: Computing methodologies Knowledge representation and reasoningCCS: Computing methodologies Neural networksCCS: Computing methodologies Natural language processingCCS: Information systems Knowledge bases

Abstract.

Fusing Knowledge Graphs with Large Language Models is crucial for knowledge-intensive tasks like knowledge graph completion. The prevailing paradigm, prefix-tuning, simply concatenates knowledge embeddings with text inputs. However, this shallow fusion overlooks the rich relational semantics within KGs and imposes a significant implicit reasoning burden on the LLM to correlate the prefix with the text. To address these, we propose Semantic-condition Tuning (SCT), a new knowledge injection paradigm comprising two key modules. First, a Semantic Graph Module employs a Graph Neural Network to extract a context-aware semantic condition from the local graph neighborhood, guided by knowledge-enhanced relations. Subsequently, this condition is passed to a Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module, which, in turn, adaptively modulates the textual embedding via two parameterized projectors, enabling a deep, feature-wise, and knowledge-aware interaction. The resulting pre-fused embedding is then fed into the LLM for fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on knowledge graph benchmarks demonstrate that SCT significantly outperforms prefix-tuning and other strong baselines. Our analysis confirms that by modulating the input representation with semantic graph context before LLM inference, SCT provides a more direct and potent signal, enabling more accurate and robust knowledge reasoning.

Keywords: 
Knowledge Graph Completion, Large Language Models, Knowledge Fusion, Graph Neural Networks, Semantic Reasoning, Fine-Tuning

1. INTRODUCTION

Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are structured representations of knowledge, formed by a collection of triples (h,r,t)(\textit{h},\textit{r},\textit{t}). With their ability to efficiently organize and encode complex semantic facts (Wang et al., 2017; Nicholson and Greene, 2020; Hogan et al., 2021), KGs have supported large-scale applications such as recommendation systems (Cui et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025), information extraction (Zhang et al., 2025), and question answering (Omar et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2025).

However, real-world KGs are inherently incomplete, which limits their utility in downstream applications (Pan et al., 2024a; Ji et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023c). Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) aims to address this challenge by inferring missing information from existing facts (Zhu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2022; Cui et al., 2025a).

Existing methods can be grouped into two main paradigms: embedding-based models and pre-trained language-based models (PLM). The first paradigm includes both geometric embedding models and methods based on graph neural networks (GNN). Geometric models such as TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), TransH (Wang et al., 2014), and RotatE (Sun et al., 2019) represent entities and relations in a continuous space. GNN-based models such as ConvE (Dettmers et al., 2018) and NBFNet (Zhu et al., 2021) aggregate multi-hop neighborhood information to encode contextual structure.

The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) (OpenAI, 2023; Zeng et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023a) has catalyzed a paradigm shift in KGC (Zhang et al., 2024a; Pan et al., 2024a; Pan et al., 2024b), which appears the second methods (PLM). Methods such as KG-BERT (Yao et al., 2019), MuKDC (Li et al., 2024a), and PKGC (Lv et al., 2022) transform triples into natural language sequences to predict triple validity. Recently, some works make a new step, employing paradigms like zero-shot reaoning (ZSR) (Brown et al., 2020) and instruction tuning (IT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) to accomplish the KGC task. The above approaches transform the KGC task into a text-based prediction of individual triples, leading to specific fundamental problems. LLMs lack the depth and precision of factual knowledge which always results in the hallucination (Zhang et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023) problem of LLMs. Besides, the structural intricacies of KGs such as subgraph structure, relational patterns, and relative entities/relations are often overlooked.

As a result, this introduces a problem: how can we effectively fuse the explicit, structured knowledge from KGs with the implicit, parametric knowledge encapsulated within LLMs??. As illustrated in Figure 1, the meaning of a relation is dynamically shaped by its surrounding semantic context. The generic relation "treats" can manifest distinct meanings under different local contexts. Aspirin’s treatment of "Fever", grounded in its role as an NSAID that reduces prostaglandins, reflects "Symptomatic Relief", whereas Oseltamivir’s therapeutic effect on the same symptom arises from its Antiviral action against the influenza virus, representing "Pathogen-Targeted Treatment". Such example reveals that fuse these richly non-textual structured information with LLMs is crucial for KGC and other knowledge-intensive tasks.

The current mainstream fusion strategy to address this is prefix-tuning. The foundational work is KoPA (Zhang et al., 2024a), projects pre-trained structural embeddings of a triple into the textual space, concatenating them as static prefix tokens. While effective, this simple concatenation represents a shallow fusion. CoK-Adapter (Li et al., 2024b) injects knowledge with both structured and text embeddings, which obtained through models like Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019a). Recent work, such as GPT-KG (Zha et al., 2025) apply GNN to prefix generation. However, these methods are merely simple prefix concatenations. This fundamentally limits the depth of integration and still places a heavy implicit reasoning burden on the LLM.

To address this fundamental gap between shallow concatenation and deep semantic integration, we propose Semantic-condition Tuning (SCT), a novel paradigm that moves beyond prefixing to achieve direct, feature-level modulation. SCT comprises two modules: 1) Semantic Graph Module focuses on explicit semantics. It employs a relational message-passing network, guided by semantic relevance scores derived from an LLM, to distill the local graph context into a potent semantic condition vector. 2) The Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module uses the graph-derived semantic condition to perform a feature-level affine transformation on the text embeddings, dynamically gating and recalibrating the textual features to align with the KG context.

By integrating these components, SCT performs fine-grained modeling of relational semantics to ensure that the input to the base LLM possess rich context-awareness. Building upon this, we fine-tune the base LLM by combining meticulously designed prompts with an adaptive embedding fusion strategy. This process enables the fine-tuned model to acutely capture the structural information of the knowledge graph. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SCT achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple standard benchmarks while maintaining superior parameter efficiency. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Semantic-Condition Tuning: We propose the first SCT framework that integrates context-awareness and adaptive embedding fusion, overcoming the limitations of existing simply prefix-tuning concatenation (Section 3).

  • •

    Semantic Graph Module: We propose a novel relation-centric message-passing mechanism where neighbor selection is guided by explicit semantic similarity scores derived from knowledge-enhanced relation descriptions (Section 3.2).

  • •

    Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module: We introduce a fusion mechanism that uses the semantic condition to learn a direct, feature-level affine transformation of the input text embeddings, achieving a deep and synergistic integration of graph context (Section 3.3).

  • •

    We demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance and high parameter efficiency of SCT on multiple benchmarks, confirming its effectiveness in leveraging semantic graph context to guide reasoning in large language models (Section 4).

2. RELATED WORK

2.1. Knowledge Graph Completion

Knowledge Graphs provide structured information for downstream tasks such as recommender systems and semantic analysis (Zhu et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024). Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) addresses the problem of KG incompleteness by predicting missing links (Pan et al., 2024a; Ibrahim et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2023).

Previously, the majority of KGC methods relied on embedding-based approaches(Long et al., 2024b; Long et al., 2024a; Ge et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2024). For instance, early geometric and bilinear models, such as TransE (Bordes et al., 2013) and ComplEx (Trouillon et al., 2016), laid the groundwork by defining simple yet effective scoring functions. To capture more sophisticated relational structures, the field subsequently advanced into more expressive geometric spaces. RotatE (Sun et al., 2019) pioneered the concept of relational rotations in the complex domain, an idea later extended by Rot-Pro (Song et al., 2021) to achieve greater precision. Other approaches focus on designing specialized geometric representations tailored for specific logical properties. For instance, HAKE (Zhang et al., 2020) leverages polar coordinates to effectively model semantic hierarchies, while BoxE (Abboud et al., 2020) employs hyper-rectangles to handle logical conjunctions. Departing from purely geometric innovations, AnKGE (Yao et al., 2023b) aim to augment the reasoning process itself, equipping models with an analogical inference mechanism to leverage similar known facts (Guo et al., 2025).

Despite their effectiveness in handling relational patterns, these models are fundamentally static where each entity and relation is assigned a fixed vector representation, and this makes them insensitive to context. To overcome it, models based on GNN have emerged, attempting to integrate contextual information from graph structures (Chang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). Methods like PathCon (Wang et al., 2021) enrich entity and relation representations by aggregating information from multi-hop paths. To mitigate the high cost of explicit path extraction, recent work CBLiP (Dutta et al., 2025) instead uses connection-biased attention to implicitly capture structural information from the local subgraph. Although GNN-based methods can capture more richer contextual semantics than embedding-based methods, they also fail to adapt to the inherent dynamism of relational formation and evolution.

2.2. LLMs for KGs research

Recently, Large Language Models(LLMs) (OpenAI, 2023; Zeng et al., 2023) have made rapid progress and demonstrated outperforming capabilities in a considerable number of text-related tasks (Zhao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a). Among the research topics of LLM, integrating LLM and KGs is a popular and important one. On one hand, KGs can anchor LLMs with factual grounding, mitigating their well-documented tendency for hallucination (Feng et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a). On the other hand, the powerful generative and inferential abilities of LLMs offer a new avenue to address long-standing KG-related tasks, including our focus KGC (Baek et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023b; Zhu et al., 2023). Our work contributes to this second direction. Existing research mainly falls into two categories of methods. One type of method refines link prediction as a textual scoring task (e.g., KG-BERT (Yao et al., 2019), SimKGC (Wang et al., 2022)). Another type of method utilizes LLMs as generative knowledge sources to distill missing facts. KG-LLaMA (Yao et al., 2023a) made the first step with a vanilla instruction tuning approach. Following this initial work, more advanced approaches like MuKDC (Li et al., 2024a) and KoPA (Zhang et al., 2024a) have emerged, demonstrating improved performance through more sophisticated prompting and multi-step reasoning strategies. However, these methods still share a common limitation: their interaction with the knowledge graph often remains at a textual or surface level (Wang et al., 2025a). Consequently, their capacity to capture the dynamic evolution of relationships based on structural context is constrained, leaving a critical gap in achieving true structure-aware reasoning. In this paper, we aim to create a more robust and effective paradigm for LLM-based knowledge graph completion.

3. METHODOLOGY

Effective Knowledge Graph Completion with LLMs requires bridging the gap between the graph’s structural context and natural language guidance. To achieve this synergy, we propose the Semantic-Condition Tuning (SCT) framework, as illustrated in Figure 2. SCT comprises two core components: a Semantic Graph Module designed to capture rich relational semantics from the KGs, and a Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module that dynamically modulates textual input embeddings based on these semantics. This mechanism yields a knowledge-aware, pre-fused representation, providing the LLM with highly informative reasoning signals.

3.1. Preliminaries

A knowledge graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is defined as a set of triples 𝒯={(h,r,t)∣h,t∈ℰ,r∈ℛ}\mathcal{T}=\{(h,r,t)\mid h,t\in\mathcal{E},r\in\mathcal{R}\}, where ℰ\mathcal{E} and ℛ\mathcal{R} represent the sets of entities and relations, respectively. The task of Knowledge Graph Completion is to infer a missing element within a given triple, such as predicting the tail entity tt for a query (h,r,?)(h,r,?). In the context of LLM-based KGC, this task is formulated as a text generation problem, where a model ℳ\mathcal{M} is prompted with a textual representation of the incomplete triple and trained to generate the correct missing entity.

Our approach, SCT, aims to enhance the model’s reasoning capability by conditioning its input on the local semantic graph structure surrounding the entities in the triple.

3.2. Semantic Graph Module

The first stage of SCT is to extract a dense, context-aware semantic representation from the graph structure. Unlike methods that simply use pre-trained entity embeddings(Zhang et al., 2024a), our Semantic Graph Module employs a carefully designed relational message-passing mechanism to derive a semantic condition vector that encapsulates the local neighborhood’s relations.

Inspired by the message passing in (Wang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025), we treat the relational structure of the KG as the primary computational graph11 1 For instance, the rule (A, is_father_of, B)∧(C, is_wife_of, A)→(C, is_mother_of, B)(\texttt{A, is\_father\_of, B})\land(\texttt{C, is\_wife\_of, A})\rightarrow(\texttt{C, is\_mother\_of, B}) is resolved by understanding relational interplay, independent of the entities’ features. Furthermore, an entity’s identity is often implicitly encoded within its local relational context, making a relation-centric focus sufficient.. Edges, representing relations, update their states by aggregating information from neighboring edges. This is more efficient and semantically indicative than node-based aggregation in KGs, where the number of relation types is significantly smaller than the number of entities.

For a given input triple (h,r,t)(h,r,t), our model first identifies the local graph neighborhoods surrounding the head entity hh and tail entity tt. To mitigate noise from indiscriminate aggregation, we introduce a Top-K selection mechanism that filters for the most semantically relevant neighbors. However, instead of relying on latent structural embeddings, our mechanism leverages the rich semantic knowledge from Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve a more robust relevance estimation.

First, in an offline pre-processing step, we perform Knowledge Enhancement for every unique relation type in the KG. We prompt a powerful LLM22 2 We use OpenAI’s GPT-4O model. Our implementation leverages the official API client from https://github.com/openai/openai-python. to generate a canonical textual description for each relation, capturing its nuanced semantic meaning. Subsequently, we use a pre-trained sentence embedding model (e.g., Sentence-BERT33 3 https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019b)) to encode these descriptions into high-quality, fixed-size semantic vectors.

During message passing, for each central edge ece_{c} (a relation incident to hh or tt), we compute its relevance to a neighboring edge en∈𝒩⁡(ec)e_{n}\in\mathcal{N}(e_{c}) using the cosine similarity between their pre-computed semantic vectors, 𝐬c\mathbf{s}_{c} and 𝐬n\mathbf{s}_{n}:

(1) Score⁡(ec,en)=𝐬c⋅𝐬n‖𝐬c‖2​‖𝐬n‖2\operatorname{Score}(e_{c},e_{n})=\frac{\mathbf{s}_{c}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{n}}{\left\|\mathbf{s}_{c}\right\|_{2}\left\|\mathbf{s}_{n}\right\|_{2}}

This approach allows the neighbor selection to be guided by explicit, rich semantic relevance rather than task-specific learned representations, leading to better generalization. The Top-K neighbors 𝒩K​(ec)\mathcal{N}_{K}(e_{c}) with the highest scores are then selected for aggregation.

Their states are first aggregated (typically via average pooling) to form a consolidated neighborhood representation 𝐬¯𝒩K​(ec)\mathbf{\bar{s}}^{\mathcal{N}_{K}(e_{c})}. We then employ a Transformer layer to refine the central edge’s state by integrating this contextual information. Specifically, the central edge’s state 𝐬cl\mathbf{s}_{c}^{l} acts as the query, while the neighborhood representation 𝐬¯𝒩K​(ec)\mathbf{\bar{s}}^{\mathcal{N}_{K}(e_{c})} serves as the key and value. This process computes the updated state for the next layer, 𝐬cl+1\mathbf{s}_{c}^{l+1}:

(2) 𝐬cl+1=TransformerLayer​(𝐬cl,𝐬¯𝒩K​(ec)).\mathbf{s}_{c}^{l+1}=\text{TransformerLayer}(\mathbf{s}_{c}^{l},\mathbf{\bar{s}}^{\mathcal{N}_{K}(e_{c})}).

This iterative update process is executed for LL layers to generate the final contextual representations of the relations surrounding the head and tail entities. These representations are then pooled to produce a single, unified, and context-aware semantic condition vector, 𝐜S∈ℝdc\mathbf{c}_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}}:

(3) 𝐜S=MeanPool​({𝐬h,iL}i∪{𝐬t,jL}j),\mathbf{c}_{S}=\text{MeanPool}(\{\mathbf{s}_{h,i}^{L}\}_{i}\cup\{\mathbf{s}_{t,j}^{L}\}_{j}),

where {𝐬h,iL}\{\mathbf{s}_{h,i}^{L}\} and {𝐬t,jL}\{\mathbf{s}_{t,j}^{L}\} are the final representations of relations in the neighborhoods of hh and tt, respectively. This vector 𝐜S\mathbf{c}_{S} serves as a rich contextual signal for the subsequent module. Notably, For link prediction, we need to mask the corresponding entity to be predicted.

3.3. Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module

The core challenge lies in seamlessly injecting the structural knowledge encapsulated in the semantic condition vector 𝐜S\mathbf{c}_{S} into the LLM’s reasoning process. Instead of naive concatenation, we introduce a condition-adaptive fusion module inspired by Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM)(Perez et al., 2018). This mechanism integrates the graph-derived context by performing a feature-level affine transformation on the LLM’s input embeddings.

Given an input prompt text represented by a sequence of embeddings 𝐗={𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱n}\mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\}, where 𝐱i∈ℝdl​l​m\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{llm}}, our fusion module transforms it into a knowledge-infused sequence 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}. This is achieved via a lightweight projector, conditioned on 𝐜S\mathbf{c}_{S}, that learns a feature-wise transformation:

(4) 𝐗′=𝐗⊙γ+β,where​γ=σ⁡(MLP1​(𝐜S)),β=MLP2​(𝐜S).\mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\mathbf{X}\odot\gamma+\beta,\quad\text{where}\;\gamma=\sigma\bigl(\text{MLP}_{1}(\mathbf{c}_{S})\bigr),\quad\beta=\text{MLP}_{2}(\mathbf{c}_{S}).

Here, ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and σ\sigma is a gating function. Two distinct MLPs project 𝐜S\mathbf{c}_{S} to generate a scaling vector γ\gamma (gate) and a shifting vector β\beta (bias), both matching the embedding dimension dl​l​md_{llm}. This transformation empowers the graph context to dynamically gate and recalibrate the textual features of each token, effectively steering the LLM’s attention towards semantics highlighted by the knowledge graph.

The resulting pre-fused embedding sequence 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime} then replaces the original embeddings and is fed into the subsequent layers of the LLM for deep processing.

3.4. Training Strategy

Our training paradigm for the SCT framework is structured into a two-stage process. This approach is designed to first endow the Semantic Graph Module with a robust understanding of graph structure and semantics, providing a strong initialization, and then to fine-tune the entire framework end-to-end, fostering a deep, synergistic alignment between the graph-based components and the Large Language Model.

3.4.1. Stage 1: Self-Supervised Pre-training of the Semantic Graph Module

To ensure the graph module possesses strong prior knowledge before the end-to-end tuning, we first pre-train it on a self-supervised link prediction task. The objective is to train the module to produce representations that can effectively discern true triples from false ones.

Given a triple (h,r,t)(h,r,t), the graph module is used to generate contextualized embeddings for the head and tail entities, denoted as 𝐞h\mathbf{e}_{h} and 𝐞t\mathbf{e}_{t}. We then define a scoring function F𝒢​(h,r,t)F_{\mathcal{G}}(h,r,t) 44 4 We provide a detailed comparison and discussion of scoring functions from traditional embedding models in our subsequent experiments. to assess the plausibility of the triple:

(5) F𝒢​(h,r,t)=⟨𝐞h,𝐞r,𝐞t⟩,F_{\mathcal{G}}(h,r,t)=\langle\mathbf{e}_{h},\mathbf{e}_{r},\mathbf{e}_{t}\rangle,

where 𝐞r\mathbf{e}_{r} is the relation semantic vector, knowledge-enhanced by an external Large Language Model (GPT-4O) and then encoded by Sentence-BERT.

The module is trained using a self-supervised objective with negative sampling. For each positive triple (h,r,t)∈𝒯(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{T}, we generate a set of kk corrupted triples 𝒯′={(hi′,r,ti′)}i=1k\mathcal{T}^{\prime}=\{(h^{\prime}_{i},r,t^{\prime}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{k} by replacing either the head or tail entity. The pre-training loss aims to maximize the scores of positive triples while minimizing those of negative ones, formulated as the negative log-likelihood loss:

(6) ℒGraph=−∑(h,r,t)∈𝒯(logσ(F𝒢(h,r,t))+∑i=1klog(1−σ(F𝒢(hi′,r,ti′)))),\mathcal{L}_{\text{Graph}}=-\sum_{(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{T}}\Biggl(\log\sigma(F_{\mathcal{G}}(h,r,t))+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\log(1-\sigma(F_{\mathcal{G}}(h^{\prime}_{i},r,t^{\prime}_{i})))\Biggr),

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. This pre-training phase endows the Semantic Graph Module with a solid foundation in understanding the KG’s structural and semantic patterns.

3.4.2. Stage 2: Alignment with the LLM

Following pre-training, the weights of the graph module serve as a powerful initialization. The entire SCT framework is then fine-tuned end-to-end on the knowledge graph completion task. The input sequence is constructed as Ss​c​t=ℐs​c​t⊕𝐗′⊕𝒜s​c​tS_{sct}=\mathcal{I}_{sct}\oplus\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\oplus\mathcal{A}_{sct}, where ℐs​c​t\mathcal{I}_{sct} is the instruction template, 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime} is the pre-fused embedding, and 𝒜s​c​t\mathcal{A}_{sct} is the ground-truth answer.

The learning objective is the standard auto-regressive, next-token prediction loss, which minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer:

(7) ℒSCT=−∑i=1|𝒮s​c​t|logP(si|s<i),\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCT}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{S}_{sct}|}\log P(s_{i}|s_{<i}),

where sis_{i} is the ii-th token in the sequence 𝒮s​c​t\mathcal{S}_{sct}. Gradients from ℒSCT\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCT}} are backpropagated to optimize the parameters of the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module and the integrated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) weights of the LLM. This process fine-tunes the fusion representations to align with the LLM’s latent space, while efficiently adapting the model’s reasoning pathways to the incoming graph semantic context. The detailed training process of stage 2 is illustrated in Algorithm 1. Finally, our inference stage can be formalized as follows:

(8) 𝒜=arg⁡max𝒜​Pℳ​(𝒜|ℐsct,𝐗′)\mathcal{A}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{A}}P_{\mathcal{M}}(\mathcal{A}|\mathcal{I}_{\text{sct}},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the answer generated by the fine-tuned model ℳ\mathcal{M}, and ℐsct\mathcal{I}_{\text{sct}} is the instruction template. Unlike other methods, SCT conditions the LLM on a semantically enriched representation that has been deeply fused with structural knowledge from the KG. This allows the LLM to perform more accurate and robust reasoning.

4. EXPERIMENTS

To evaluate the effectiveness of SCT, we designed a series of experiments to address the following research questions:

  • •

    RQ1: How significantly can SCT enhance LLMs’ performance in KGC tasks??

  • •

    RQ2: What are the distinct contributions of SCT’s key components to its overall performance?

  • •

    RQ3: How Does Context from Semantic Graphs Enhance the Reasoning of LLMs?

4.1. Experiment Settings

4.1.1. Datasets.

We evaluate our SCT framework on three widely recognized KGC benchmark datasets:

WN18RR (Dettmers et al., 2018) and FB15k-237 (Toutanova and Chen, 2015): These datasets are used for the link prediction task. Both have inverse relations removed, making them standards for evaluating complex reasoning abilities.

UMLS, CoDeX-S and FB15k-237N (Lv et al., 2022): These are employed for the triple classification task. It provides high-quality negative samples for each triple, making them ideal for assessing a model’s ability to distinguish factual correctness. Detailed statistics for these datasets are provided in Table 1.

4.1.2. Baselines.

Our selection of baselines covers a wide spectrum of representative methods, from traditional KGE models to the latest LLM-based approaches. Many results are directly cited from the SSQR (Lin et al., 2024a) and Kopa (Zhang et al., 2024a) to maintain consistency.

For Link Prediction: We compare against (1) Emb-based Methods: TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), CompGCN (Vashishth et al., 2020), AdaProp (Zhang et al., 2024b), MA-GNN (Xu et al., 2023), TCRA (Guo et al., 2024a), and DiffusionE (Ca et al., 2024); (2) LLM-based Methods: KICGPT (Wei et al., 2023), CSProm-KG-CD (Li et al., 2023), ARR (Chen et al., 2024), KG-FIT (Jiang et al., 2024), MKGL (Guo et al., 2024b), SSQR-LLaMA2 (Lin et al., 2024b).

For Triple Classification: We compare against (1) Emb-based Methods: TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), DistMult (Yang et al., 2015), ComplexE (Trouillon et al., 2016), and RotatE (Sun et al., 2019); (2) LLM-based Methods: KG-LLaMA (Yao et al., 2023a), KG-Alpaca (Yao et al., 2023a), KOPA (Zhang et al., 2024a), and SSQR-LLaMA2 (Lin et al., 2024b).

4.1.3. Evaluation Metrics

Link Prediction: We report Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Hits@N. Triple Classification: We report Accuracy (Acc), Precision (P), Recall (R), and F1-Score.

4.1.4. Implementation Details

Our SCT framework is implemented on top of the Alpaca-7B. The Semantic Graph Module utilizes a 2-layer Transformer architecture, with the number of neighbors Top-K set to 10. First, the SGM is pre-trained for 20 epochs on the self-supervised link prediction task. Next, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) with a rank of 64 to fine-tune the LLM. The number of epochs is searched in {3, 4, 5} and the learning rate is tuned in {1​e−4,3​e−4,5​e−41e^{-4},3e^{-4},5e^{-4}}. We use the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with a fixed batch size of 12. We conducted all the experiments with Nvidia A800-80GB GPUs.

4.2. Overall Performance Comparison: RQ1

4.2.1. Link Prediction

The classic link prediction is essentially a ranking problem, i.e., determining the rank of the correct tail entity within a set of candidates. To facilitate fine-tuning for this task, we formulate the instruction template ℐs​c​t\mathcal{I}_{sct} as detailed in the following prompt. Concurrently, we align our candidate entity generation method with that of SSQR-LLaMA255 5 In their fine-tuning stage, the method employs the pre-trained AdaProp to generate 20 candidates per query, chosen for its robust and balanced performance..

The main results for the link prediction task are presented in Table 2. Our SCT framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across both the WN18RR and FB15k-237 benchmarks.

On the WN18RR dataset, SCT consistently outperforms the strongest baseline, SSQR-LLaMA2, achieving relative gains of 2.2% in MRR, 2.4% in Hits@1, and 2.6% in Hits@3. The performance advantage is even more pronounced on the larger and more complex FB15k-237 dataset, where SCT achieves a substantial 4.9% relative improvement in MRR. Furthermore, it records notable increases of 1.6% in Hits@1 and 4.4% in Hits@10.

These significant gains, particularly in the comprehensive MRR metric, underscore SCT’s effectiveness. This success is attributable to our core components. The Semantic Graph Module provides the LLM with rich, context-aware signals, while the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module efficiently injects this structural knowledge. This synergy empowers the LLM to better comprehend and reason about complex facts, leading to superior ranking performance.

4.2.2. Triple Classification.

To further assess the generalization capabilities of our framework, we evaluated SCT on the triple classification task across three diverse datasets: UMLS, CoDeX-S, and FB15K-237N. The instruction template for this task, ℐs​c​t\mathcal{I}_{sct}, is different from that of link prediction, as shown in the above prompt.

The results, detailed in Table 3, affirm that SCT consistently achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance, validating its robustness beyond link prediction.

On the UMLS dataset, SCT establishes a new state-of-the-art by securing the top performance across all metrics, achieving an accuracy of 93.15% and an F1-score of 93.18%. This leadership extends to the larger and more complex FB15k-237N dataset, where our model again leads the field, securing the highest accuracy (78.02%), precision (71.10%), and F1-score (80.93%). The top-ranking F1-score on this benchmark signifies an optimal balance, while the superior precision highlights the model’s high confidence in its positive classifications. This consistent superiority on two datasets with distinct characteristics underscores the model’s strong capacity to discern factual plausibility.

On the CoDeX-S dataset, SCT demonstrates highly competitive results, notably achieving the highest precision at 78.52%. While its other metrics are on par with the strong KoPA baseline, this top-tier precision underscores SCT’s ability to make high-confidence positive predictions. The overall strong performance across these varied benchmarks confirms that our method of fusing rich semantic context with language models provides a powerful and generalizable foundation for knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.

4.3. Ablation study: RQ2

To verify the effectiveness of our proposed modules, we develop two distinct model variants for ablation studies:

  • •

    w/o Semantics: We remove the Semantic Graph Module and replace it with pre-trained embeddings from a conventional Knowledge Graph Embedding model.

  • •

    w/o Fusion: We remove the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module. Instead, the semantic graph condition vector is injected into the LLM by concatenating it as a prefix to the input text embeddings.

The results, presented in Table 4, unequivocally demonstrate that both modules are critical to the success of the SCT framework.

Effectiveness of the Semantic Graph Module.

The “w/o Semantics” variant, which replaces our module with standard KGEs, shows a significant performance decline on both datasets. On the more complex FB15k-237, MRR drops from 0.471 to 0.433, and more critically, Hits@1 plummets from 0.380 to 0.327. This substantial drop validates the superiority of our dynamically generated, context-aware semantic condition over static, pre-trained embeddings. It confirms the importance of capturing rich, local relational semantics to provide the LLM with a high-quality signal for reasoning.

Effectiveness of the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module.

The impact of the fusion mechanism is even more pronounced. The “w/o Fusion” variant, which reverts to a simpler prefix-tuning approach, exhibits the most severe performance degradation. On FB15k-237, MRR and Hits@1 decrease dramatically by 0.062 and 0.081, respectively. This massive decline across all metrics confirms the limitations of shallow fusion and strongly validates our central hypothesis: the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module, by enabling a deep, feature-wise interaction, provides a far more effective and potent mechanism for injecting structural knowledge into the LLM.

Finally, we briefly analyze the choice of the scoring function, F𝒢​(h,r,t)F_{\mathcal{G}}(h,r,t), used in our pre-training stage. As shown in Table 6, we compared several classic scoring functions on the FB15k-237 dataset. The experimental results clearly indicate that the RotatE-style function yields the best performance across all metrics, achieving the highest MRR of 0.471. Simpler models like DistMult and a standard MLP led to a discernible drop in performance. This empirical comparison validates our selection of RotatE for the final SCT.

The superiority of RotatE can likely be attributed to its inherent ability to model complex relational patterns. This powerful inductive bias allows the model to update higher-quality embeddings during pre-training. As a result, when the Semantic Graph Module aggregates information from the neighborhood represented by these superior embeddings, it generates a more informative semantic graph condition vector. This provides the LLM with a richer, more structured signal that ultimately boosts performance.

4.4. Analysis of Semantics: RQ3

In this section, we will conduct detailed experiments on the semantic graph module. First, we conduct a sensitivity analysis on the hyperparameter Top-K, which defines the size of the local semantic neighborhood for each node. As illustrated in Figure 3, the model’s performance, measured by MRR and Hit@1, peaks at K=10 with scores of 0.471 and 0.380, respectively. This result highlights the importance of an appropriate neighborhood size. A small K (e.g., K=4) may limit the model’s ability to capture sufficient semantic and structural features due to inadequate neighborhood information. Conversely, a large K (e.g., K=32) can introduce irrelevant noise and lead to the over-smoothing issue.

Second, a core innovation of our SGM is the knowledge enhancement, which uses an LLM to generate rich semantic descriptions for relations before they are embedded. To quantify the impact of this enhancement, we create a model variant:

SCT w/o Relation Enhancement: In this variant, we bypass the LLM-based description generation step. When computing the semantic vectors for neighbor selection, we directly encode the names of the relations using the same pre-trained Sentence-BERT.

As shown in Table 7, removing the knowledge-enhanced descriptions leads to a significant performance drop across all metrics. This strongly validates the importance of our knowledge enhancement. Simply using relation names provides a weak semantic signal.

To demonstrate the importance of semantics and the role of our module. We examine the query (Barack Obama, /government/
politician/government_positions_held…, ?), which describes the geographical or administrative scope of a political position. Table 5 contrasts the top-5 retrieved neighbor relations before and after applying knowledge enhancement, clearly showing a shift from lexical matching to semantic relevance.

Without knowledge enhancement, neighbor ranking is limited by superficial lexical overlap. Gov Position (Title) and (Sessions) rank highly because they share long string prefixes with the query relation, a method that fails to capture deeper semantics.

With knowledge enhancement, the ranking logic shifts to true semantic relevance. The most crucial change is the emergence and high ranking of Person (Nationality), which correctly links the concept of "jurisdiction" in the query to "nationality"—a deep insight unattainable by pure lexical matching. Concurrently, the ranking of related concepts like Person (Profession) is boosted, while noisy signals like Person (Places Lived) are effectively suppressed.

In summary, this case study demonstrates that SGM can transcend shallow text matching, acting as an intelligent filter to construct a more semantically coherent context vector (cSc_{S}), thereby providing more precise and effective signals for LLM reasoning.

5. Conclusion

In this paper, we propose Semantic-Condition Tuning (SCT), a novel framework designed to overcome the limitations of shallow fusion in existing methods for integrating KGs with LLMs. SCT moves beyond the simple prefix-tuning paradigm, achieving a deep and synergistic injection of structured knowledge and textual information through two core modules. First, the Semantic Graph Module leverages LLM-enhanced relation semantics to distill a context-aware semantic condition vector from the local graph structure. Subsequently, this vector is used by the Condition-Adaptive Fusion Module to perform a feature-level dynamic affine transformation on the input text embeddings, completing a deep pre-fusion of knowledge before the LLM’s inference process.

Extensive experiments on multiple knowledge graph benchmarks demonstrate that SCT achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance. Research confirms that its Semantic-Condition Tuning injects knowledge from KGs into LLMs more effectively. Despite its promising performance, SCT still faces challenges, notably limited reasoning depth and insufficient adaptability to dynamic knowledge graphs. Our future work will address these limitations in three key directions. First, we plan to introduce a hierarchical semantic condition generation mechanism to enhance reasoning depth. Second, we will incorporate temporal awareness into the model. Finally, we will explore extending our framework to more complex scenarios, such as temporal knowledge graphs.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
